course_title: IC Design Process: Beginner's Overview to VLSI

slides.title: IC Design: Connecting Code to Silicon
points: Bridge HDL code to physical circuits
slides.speaker_notes: This course simplifies the journey from your HDL code to actual silicon. We'll connect the dots across the entire VLSI design process: from RTL to verification, synthesis, and physical design. Our focus is a theoretical overview, not specific coding.

slides.title: Understanding ICs & SOCs
points: IC: numerous circuits on tiny silicon
SOC: entire system on one chip
slides.speaker_notes: An IC packs electronic circuits onto a tiny silicon plate. An SOC integrates a complete system onto one chip, often with billions of transistors. ICs can be analog or digital; we focus on digital designs for this course.

slides.title: Evolution of IC Technology
slides.speaker_notes: Circuits moved from vacuum tubes to transistors in 1947, sparking the Integrated Circuit concept. This evolved through SSI, MSI, and LSI. Now, VLSI, or Very Large-Scale Integration, is the standard for all high-density chips, housing billions of transistors.

slides.title: Digital Circuit Building Blocks
slides.speaker_notes: Digital circuits process binary data using transistors as on/off switches. We have combinational circuits, dependent only on current inputs, and sequential circuits, which use memory for past inputs. Key building blocks are logic gates and flip-flops, which store single bits of data.

slides.title: The Transistor Foundation
points: Every digital circuit is a transistor network
Modern ICs house billions of transistors
slides.speaker_notes: Flip-flops are built from logic gates, and all logic gates are made from transistors – typically CMOS. Thus, every digital circuit, no matter its complexity, is ultimately a vast network of transistors. Modern ICs integrate billions of these fundamental switches.

slides.title: Why We Use HDLs
points: Model circuits at a higher level
slides.speaker_notes: Directly designing complex, transistor-level circuits is impractical. Hardware Description Languages, or HDLs, are essential. They allow us to model and design digital circuits at a higher, abstract level. This hides the overwhelming transistor details, simplifying the entire IC design process.
